Post-mortem

How we missed the obvious

Our score was wrong. Hand-built arm C scored 0.957 against his picture and Meshy scored 0.915, yet measured in 3D, C is 4.3 cm off Meshy's body on average and our own learned build is 2.4 cm off. The score rewarded a wrong model over a right one, because his picture is not a front view.

Seven cues, all leaning the same way

  1. The head shows its side plane; the nose points right.
  2. The tank top's neckline sits off the shoulders' centre.
  3. The far shoulder shows its top and outer plane.
  4. The far forearm shows its outer side; the near one shows its front.
  5. The shorts show a side panel on one side only.
  6. One foot points out about 45°.
  7. The other foot points at the camera.

The camera is turned about 23° (two checks agree: 24° and 23°). The brief told every arm "the reference is a front view". Agents did log "head turned 7°" and "foot turned 43°", but each was written down as pose and nobody was allowed to question the brief. So every arm built a square body and stretched its outline until a square camera matched a turned picture. Scoring only that one outline could never catch it, and the side and back we added came from the Midjourney turnaround, which is itself a guess.

Every build is too thin, and the back is missing

Meshy's body, painted by how far each build is from it. Blue means ours falls short. Front-to-back, the hand builds fall short twice as much as side-to-side: chest depth 35 to 45 cm against Meshy's 51. The back of every hand build is dark blue: no trapezius, no lats, no shoulder blades, no spine curve. Arms are the worst region (3 to 4 cm thin all round); head and thighs, the parts the picture shows squarely, were fine.

What we did to Meshy's mesh to get G

  1. Turned him square (−24°), stood him on the ground, scaled him to 2.0 m.
  2. Welded the vertices Meshy splits at its texture seams and fixed the normals. Without this the cut-down mesh cracked.
  3. Sliced the body every 2 cm into rings and tracked them into named parts: torso, deltoids, arms, hands, legs.
  4. Tied every vertex to its ring, so a change said in words ("forearms 20% thicker") moves the surface.
  5. Cut to 10% of the faces, flat shading, colours by height band (skin, tank top, shorts).

None of those steps reads his picture. The shape is all Meshy's.

Meshy against his actual picture

His picture, Meshy turned 24°, and the two outlines over each other. Meshy's hands are smaller and set higher, its feet shorter, its head a little narrower, and the tank top's rolled trim is smoothed away. His picture's camera is also lower and a little wider than ours, which makes his feet and legs bigger.

Getting good, then getting cheap

  1. Measure the camera before modelling. Read the cues, estimate the turn, and check it against the cutout. Never assume "front view".
  2. Score in 3D and in the picture's own camera. One outline is not a score.
  3. Take depth from a skeleton and a body model, never from the outline.
  4. Build the back on purpose, from the anatomy checklist.
  5. Score anatomy region by region, like the table above.

Brute #2 test, scored against his Meshy model: brute #1's settings as they are, 0.737; refitted, 0.762; a guess from his picture alone, by an agent that saw no 3D, 0.718. The settings carry real knowledge, but one picture still doesn't give depth. Once a picture-only guess with these rules reaches the refitted score, a new figure costs nothing but our own Blender time, and Meshy becomes an occasional audit.

Round 4 · Meshy as the target

The scaling version

Meshy made a near-perfect 3D model of him from his picture in about 40 seconds (arm M). Arm G learns from it: every 2 cm of height the Meshy body is cut into rings, one stack per named part (torso, each arm, each leg, the hands). The rings are the recipe. They are written down in numbers and in words, they drive Meshy's own surface like a cage, and Blender takes the result to whatever polygon count we ask for.

  1. LearnRead the hero mesh into named parts and rings, and write it down in numbers and in words.python3 scale/learn.py → spec.json, spec.md
  2. Say itAsk for a change in body words. A person or a model picks the op, region and amount; the words are kept with the edit.python3 scale/edit.py scale forearm --width 1.2 --depth 1.2 --say "make his forearms 20% bigger"
  3. BuildThe rings move Meshy's vertices, then Decimate sets the polygon count. Every step saves a screenshot.python3 scale/deform.py --spec spec --ratio 0.1 --shots
  4. CheckRead it back in words (measure) and against the hero from four sides plus his picture's camera. Undo is one command.python3 scale/edit.py measure forearm python3 scale/edit.py undo

Scoreboard

Lower loss is better; higher IoU is better. Side IoU compares his profile with the Midjourney turnaround of the same guy, which is where depth shows. Per-part squares fill from pale to green as each chunk's own silhouette IoU rises: head, chest, right arm, left arm, hips, legs.

    ArmMethodSilhouette IoULossSide IoUPer partTimeCostStatus

    The arms

    Same reference, same six chunks, same Blender recipe kit and the same budget per job. Only how the work is split and ordered changes.

    The six chunks

    In arm A each job sees only its crop below. In the other arms each job sees the whole figure and owns one chunk.

    What we measure

    Silhouette IoU
    Overlap of the model's outline with the reference outline, from the same front camera. 1.0 is a perfect match.
    Leads
    Best all-round likeness among the hand-built arms: the average of the front, side and back outline scores, so getting his depth right counts as much as matching the picture. Meshy (M) and the scaling version (G) are the target and what we learn from it, so they aren't ranked against them.
    Loss
    The paper-warrior image loss: silhouette, outline distance, structure, facet edges and tone, weighted into one number. 0 is perfect.
    Per-part score
    Silhouette IoU inside each chunk's box, so a great torso can't hide a missing hand.
    Time and cost
    Wall-clock from first job to assembled model, and the model spend for all of an arm's jobs.
    Fidelity check
    Pass or fail by eye: this figure, not an inspired one. Five fingers per hand, a face with brow, nose and jaw, toes on bare feet.
